A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoJudge and provide readable main text, algorithms, equations, figures and complete appendices. Content can be reliably matched across v1's Appendices A–D and v2's expanded Appendices A–L.

before.justification: V1 reports original GSM8K and LiveCodeBench evaluations, classifier ablations, precision comparisons and cross-task transfer results.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark and classifier results, plus GPU timing, window-size tuning, offloading and inference-instability experiments.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, logistic-regression classification and the inference rejection-override rule are retained. The target-only features used by v2's vLLM implementation were already evaluated as an option in v1 Appendix B. API-based execution relocates target generation without introducing a new mining rule.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GSM8K mathematical reasoning and LiveCodeBench release_v5 programming tasks, including all difficulty subsets and cross-task classifier transfer. Larger models, eight-shot prompting and offloading change experimental configurations rather than task coverage. MMLU-Pro appears only in v2's references and license list, without reported evaluation.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain lossless speculative decoding, top-K acceptance and standalone model references; classifier comparisons retain logistic regression, random forest and MLP. V1's 'Leviathan' label corresponds to speculative decoding in v2. The new timing tables use lossless or autoregressive inference references, and neither version directly evaluates Judge Decoding.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands model configurations to larger Llama pairs and Qwen, adds eight-shot GSM8K evaluations, and introduces vLLM timing, offloading and window-size tuning over 8–64 tokens. Appendix I adds a 132-example accuracy diagnostic. Reported classifier settings also change: the regularization search ends at 10^-7 rather than 10^-9, and Appendix B specifies max_iter=500 and min_samples_leaf=0.001 instead of v1's stated defaults.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of whether speedups survive individually optimized window sizes, how offloading affects efficiency, and whether lossless vLLM accuracy changes with window size (Appendices G–I). Existing classifier, embedding, precision and cross-task analyses remain, with revised results rather than merely relocated displays.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. V2 acknowledges latency variability but introduces no uncertainty-estimation procedure. The existing five-fold LiveCodeBench evaluation is retained.

E6.justification: V2 adds larger-model and Qwen results and substantial timing evidence, including 94.6 versus 49.2 tokens/s for AutoJudge and speculative decoding in Table 1. Retained results also change: the 1B/8B LiveCodeBench target reference moves from 16.25% to 16.81% (v1 Figure 3; v2 Figure 4), and random-forest AUC changes from 0.712 to 0.768 (v1 Figure 4; v2 Figure 5). These are reported updates, not established improvements under identical settings.

T1.justification: The answer-equivalence and mismatch definitions, search reasoning, important-token guarantee and conditional Gumbel sampling construction are retained. V2's statement that sampling remains to be tested adds an empirical qualification, not new mathematics or a proof.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds accepted-token gains for the 1B/8B setup and defers larger-model and optimized-runtime experiments. V2 makes completed vLLM integration and measured GPU acceleration explicit headline contributions, including an approximately twofold speedup claim with a 70B target and experiments with 405B. The central annotation-free mining claim remains unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications concerning untested equivalence judging for open-ended tasks, token-mining cost, hardware-dependent speedups and latency variability. Appendices I and K discuss backend-dependent accuracy and API retokenization effects. These substantially expand the applicability and implementation limitations beyond v1's existing task-transfer and precision discussions.

D1.justification: V2 documents vLLM integration, software versions, batch size, target-only classifier inputs, GPU configurations, FP8 use and parallelization. Appendices J–L add per-example processing times, API-based mining instructions, an approximately $800 API-cost example and licensing information. V1 mainly supplied classifier-training details and the repository link.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for Qwen2.5, Llama 3, software, MMLU-Pro and recent inference-reproducibility work. It also explicitly attributes the missing direct Judge Decoding comparison to unavailable code and annotations. Positioning AutoJudge as an automated extension of Judge Decoding remains intact.

P1.justification: V2 edits wording throughout, rewrites the abstract and experimental overview, adds an explicit contribution list and acknowledgements, and renames Method and Discussion to Method Overview and Conclusion. Appendix D is subdivided, but the main narrative order and much of the method and existing appendix prose remain.

P2.justification: V1's combined benchmark Figure 3 becomes separate GSM8K and LiveCodeBench figures with additional model panels. V2 redraws existing analysis plots and adds a substantial suite of runtime and diagnostic tables. The original schematic and token examples are retained and relocated, distinguishing these moves from the new displays.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's central lack of practical runtime validation through GPU timing, larger-model experiments and comparisons with individually tuned windows, while substantially improving implementation and cost documentation. Table 5 still reports useful speedups after baseline tuning. Accuracy and throughput come from different backends, and some settings conflict between prose and tables, limiting the precision of the speed–quality claims. Nevertheless, the added validation and transparency provide a substantial overall improvement.
